The line beginning 'In Barraeus's edition' is the modern editor's footnote printed in the text, not part of Paulinus's letter; it is translated as given. Scanning errors silently corrected include 'rore recreatur', 'de actu vestro', 'sui tribuat', 'cur suus ad vitem, asinae vero pullus ad cilicium', 'cincinnulos' (for 'rucinnulos'), 'junctus amicitia', and the garbled Greek of Gen. 49:11, read as καὶ τῇ ἕλικι τὸν πῶλον τῆς ὄνου αὐτοῦ. In Preface IV, 'Quaedam referuntur ad Judam' seems truncated; one expects a following 'quaedam ad Christum' ('some to Christ'). The edition's marginal conjecture 'adorarunt' for 'adorant' in Book I.1 is reflected in the past tense 'were made'. In Preface III the edition suggests 'peragi' for 'pati'; 'bear' follows the printed text.

In 1.2 'potentia beatorum' ('power of the blessed') is odd; possibly corrupt (perhaps 'bellatorum', 'of warriors'). γοσικως is read as φυσικῶς ('naturally'), τροπικής as τροπικῶς ('figuratively'). The reference 'Act. 3' for 'destroyed him who had the power of death' is actually Heb. 2:14. Scripture references 'Joan. 25' and 'Luc. 12' are scanning errors, corrected to John 15 and Luke 19.

Line 1.5: the citation 'Gen. 49. 41' is a scanning error for 49:11. Line 1.1a: the sentence 'Haec super eos qui lacte alantur... super illos, qui tanquam parvuli adhuc lacte indigent' appears corrupt; translated literally with bracketed supplements, but the sense (the perfect, white-toothed, set above those still fed on milk) is uncertain. 'pro possibilitate sumendi' differs from the Vulgate 'pro consuetudine' in Heb. 5:14. Line 1.2a: '[Forte bonam]' is an editorial conjecture in the printed text ('perhaps good'), rendered in brackets. Several scriptural references in the edition are inaccurate (e.g. 'Rom. 11' for Rom. 6:10–11, 'Phil. 4' for the spirit of adoption, Rom. 8:15; 'Prov. 5' for Prov. 1:5; '2 Cor. 9' for 1 Cor. 9:26; '1 Cor. 10' for 2 Cor. 10:5; 'Matth. 19' for Matt. 18:3); they are kept as printed except where corrected in the translation for 2 Cor. 10. 'Gratifici' rendered 'gracious', in keeping with the following play on gratia.

Paulinus's letter: 'quia remeaturus ad Orientem' read as referring to Rufinus's return East; the variant 'filii Babylonis' for 'filia Babylonis' is noted by the edition. 'repulsoue metu, aa verecundiam' read as 'repulsusve metu ad verecundiam'; the sense is uncertain. 'propter operit' is corrupt, perhaps for 'propter opus' ('about the work'), and the rendering is tentative. The citation 'Matth. 15' for the parable of the two sons should be Matt. 21; 'Gen. 34' for Reuben's incest should be Gen. 35:22. In 2.1, 'quale est et illud' may conceal a lacuna before 'qua vel mors': 'mors' is read as 'mores' (conduct), and '[rebuke]' is supplied for the sense. 'Agar' is rendered 'Hagar'.

Simeon/Levi §1: 'Emmor filium Sychem' read as Hamor and his son Shechem (literally 'Hamor son of Shechem'). Same section: 'furorem temeritate' taken as 'fury for its rashness'; text may be corrupt. Simeon/Levi §2: 'scriptum est bis' taken as a slip; 'bis' left untranslated. Same section: 'ereden- tium' read as 'credentium'. §3: 'Ilas' read as 'Has'. Zebulun §2: 'posteaqmim' read as 'posteaquam'. Zebulun §2: 'matarum' read as 'malarum'. Zebulun §2: 'excutit' rendered 'stretches himself out' for sense, alongside 'extendit'. Issachar §1: 'duae semi tribus' rendered 'two tribes', since 'semi' seems corrupt. Scripture references 'Ibid. 4' etc. in Reuben §3 are given as 2 Cor. 4 and 1 Cor. 15.

2.4.2: '[rudus ventris' is read as 'fructus ventris'. The Ps. 126 quotation is abbreviated in the text, and 'inheritance' is supplied from the psalm. The reference '1 Cor. 5' is read as 1 Cor. 3. 2.4.3: The clause '(ut est totius animae languor) ira et furore errantem' seems corrupt or lacunose; it is translated literally. 2.5.3: The bracketed '[Forte poenitentiam]' is the edition's own conjecture; it is kept as a bracketed alternative. 'Ignorantiam futuram nesciebat' is awkward and probably corrupt; it is rendered by sense as 'did not know ... would come'. The citation 'Luc. 18' for 'Propitius esto' belongs to Matt. 16.

Gad 1: 'Pirateriumatentabit' read as 'Piraterium tentabit'; 'Arabiae panibus' read as 'partibus' (parts). Gad 2 end: 'a tentat' read as 'ipse tentat'; the object is unexpressed. Gad 3: 'simili editione' perhaps for 'simili ratione'; 'e reddit conversum' read as 'se reddit conversum'. Asher 1: 'pioptcr' read as 'propter'. Asher 3: 'sapientium' read as 'sapientiam'. Naphtali 1: 'Arborar emissa' read as 'Arbor remissa'. Naphtali 2: 'so(??)iat(??)' read as 'sociatur'. Asher 2: the citation 'Joan. 1' is presumably John 6. Dan 3: the citation of 1 Cor. 12 is properly 2 Cor. 12.

Several scanning errors read silently (e.g. 'lime' as 'tunc', 'vacabitur' as 'vocabitur', 'die designabamus' as 'dici designabamus', 'quaedam' with stray footnote mark taken as 'a certain [woman]'). 'Per traducem' rendered 'through a kind of vine-layer' (tradux = a vine shoot trained across). Some scriptural references in the edition appear misnumbered (e.g. 1 Cor. 13 for 2 Cor. 13:4; Job 14; Ps. 106 for Ps. 109); left as printed.

Section 3: the 'Zelo vos Dei zelo' citation is 2 Cor. 11:2, though the edition prints '1. Cor. 11'; 'Ne laudaveris quemquam ante obitum' is Ecclus. 11:28 ('Eccl. II.'). 'per fidei prof(??)c um' read as profectum; 'post e(??)s' read as errores; 'tu (??) quum' read as tunc quum. Section 1: variant 'efferuntur' for 'offeruntur' noted by the edition. Section 2: 'e in legem non pervenerit' is likely corrupt (Rom. 9:31 'in legem justitiae non pervenit'); translated with an implied 'though'. The sentence beginning 'haec nunc quae...' lacks a main verb before 'Tunc omnis salvus fiet Israel'; rendered as continuing into it.

The figure '50' in the text is a printed page or column number and has been omitted. 'in(??)se' is read as 'nisi'. 'arte cognoscit' is read as 'certe cognoscet' (the variant 'cognoscent' is noted in the edition). 'sacramento' is read as 'sacramenta'. 'Ethnicam' is read as 'Ethicam' (ethical); the scanned text would mean 'pagan'. The final clause 'maximum mihi dona delictum' seems corrupt; it is translated as if it read 'maximum mihi duco delictum' ('I would count it a very great fault in myself').

nodes.text: THE TWO BOOKS OF TYRANNIUS RUFINUS OF AQUILEIA, PRESBYTER, ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS.

"I have sent a note to Rufinus the presbyter, the companion of holy Melania on the spiritual way, a truly holy man, devoutly learned, and for that reason bound to me by close affection." St Paulinus, Letter 28, to Sulpicius Severus.
TO BROTHER RUFINUS
PAULINUS [sends] greeting.

I. Even a short letter from you, who are one in heart with us, is a great refreshment to us, as a thirsty field is revived by dew when rivers fail. So we confess that we were refreshed by your letter, short as it was, yet still yours, [brought] by the servant of our common sons; but we were also distressed again, because you still remain in the heat of anxiety and in uncertainty about delays, and have decided to make for Rome. May the Lord grant that we may be gladdened by the Lord as soon as possible about your affairs, so that, as we suffer with you in your anxieties, so we may rejoice with you in your cheerfulness, and may yet begin to hope for the fruit of your presence, if you begin to be certain of your own decision, or of the Lord's good pleasure concerning you.

II. Indeed, as for your kindly urging me, with that affection with which you love us as yourself, to take up the study of Greek letters more attentively, I accept it gladly, but I cannot fulfil it, unless perhaps the Lord helps my desires, so that I may enjoy your company longer. For how shall I be able to make progress in a language I do not know, if there is no one from whom I may learn what I do not know? For I believe that in the translation of St Clement, besides the other shortcomings of my talent, you noticed above all this poverty of my inexperience: that some passages, where I could not understand or render the words, I translated by grasping the sense instead, or, to speak more truly, by guessing. So I need the mercy of God all the more, that he may grant me a fuller abundance of himself, since for a poor man it will be riches even to gather the crumbs falling from the rich man's table with the eager mouth of a hungry heart.

In Barraeus's edition 'Bishop of Nola' was wrongly added; for Paulinus had not yet obtained the dignity of bishop at that time, but served only in the rank of presbyter. That is, in the year 398, in which he wrote this letter to Rufinus. Accordingly Brunius, the editor of Paulinus himself, learned as he is in other respects, is also mistaken in making it almost a full decade later, believing it written around the year 408, following, as it seems, the reasoning of Tillemont. There is no reason why we should demonstrate this date of it at greater length after the arguments of the distinguished Fontanini, which can be read in the preceding Life of Rufinus, Book and chapter II. There is even less reason for us to defend the genuineness of the letter itself against the suspicions of learned men who have charged it with spuriousness; for the matter itself cries out that nothing other than the odium attached to the name of Rufinus, to whom it is addressed, was the cause, so that St Paulinus should not seem joined to him in friendship.

III. Indeed, at the time when this letter was being written, there fell under my eyes, coming up in the reading set before me, that chapter of Genesis in which Judah is blessed by Jacob. And since the Lord had given this most opportune occasion, I decided after some time to knock at the doors of your heart. So if you love me, or rather since you love me much, I ask you to write to me how you understand the blessing of the patriarchs itself. And if you yourself know any things in them difficult in sense and worth knowing, please let me know them; but especially about that passage in which it says: Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's foal to the haircloth (Gen. 49:11): who is his foal, and who the ass's foal; and why is his own [foal] bound to the vine, but the ass's foal to the haircloth?
PREFACE TO THE BOOK ON THE BLESSINGS OF JUDAH BY RUFINUS OF AQUILEIA, PRESBYTER, TO PAULINUS THE PRESBYTER

I. The more I excuse myself to you and declare myself unfit to answer the things you ask, the more insistently you question me and the harder the things you inquire into; and as if you had caught the fault of a slow ox, you dig with more persistent goads into its hesitating shoulders and its back as it gives ground. Hence it follows that you must also learn this at once: that even if, at least with lowered neck, we can move the burden of the yoke you lay on us, yet we nowhere have the means to cross open and wide-spreading plains at a quicker pace, with the resources of a more abundant style that pours itself out over broad stretches. Therefore bear with us if perhaps we choose to arrive where you call us with somewhat slower steps.

II. You ask us how that is to be understood which is written in Genesis about the patriarch Judah, that his father Israel, while foretelling to each of his sons what he foresaw would happen, said of him among other things: Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's foal to the branch of the vine (Gen. 49:11). Where you wrote: And his ass's foal to the haircloth, in Greek it reads thus: καὶ τῇ ἕλικι τὸν πῶλον τῆς ὄνου αὐτοῦ. The Greeks call ἕλιξ not so much the branch of the vine (as our copies have it) as those little curls, as it were, by which it leans on the branches of a tree, or on stakes, or on whatever supports, which farmers, I think, call tendrils: secure in these bonds and without danger of falling, the branch is either weighed down with fruit or stretched out in roving length. I think, then, that this very Greek word was placed in the Latin copies long ago, as were some others too, and in the course of time was taken by copyists who did not understand it to stand for cilicium [haircloth].

III. And in this the translator's error is easily corrected; but it is not so easy to find the sense of the meaning itself, unless the whole chapter is taken into account. Yet a treatment of this whole chapter would find something fuller and clearer if it took its starting point from the beginning of the Blessings themselves. That certainly requires no little leisure and time, and, to speak more truly, it demands a mind illuminated by the Holy Spirit. So, as far as the modesty of our understanding avails, or time allows, or those permit who are pressing for the replies to Origen, with such brevity as so great a matter could bear, out of that love by which you bid us confide in you about everything, and without prejudice to those who may be able to judge something better, we set out what seems to us meanwhile about this chapter.

IV. I know that very many interpret this chapter of the Lord in such a way as to assert that nothing of what is said pertains to the patriarch Judah, because he is nowhere shown to have slept like a lion, nor to have been roused like a lion's whelp, nor will the nations be proved to have hoped in him in any way. But when it says: A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes for whom it is laid up, that is, the kingdom, and in him the nations will hope: since 'until he comes for whom it is laid up, in whom the nations will hope' is plainly said of Christ, we are forced without doubt to understand that he from whose seed a leader will not fail until Christ comes is someone other than Christ. For it is not fitting that he should be understood as Christ from whose seed a leader will not fail until Christ comes, since that leadership in fact failed at the coming of Christ. And this very thing was a sign that he had come for whom it is laid up, that is, Christ. Some things refer to Judah; as in very many other places, so in this chapter too it is to be understood that the exposition should be guided by alternating interpretation, and that the interruption of the historical understanding reveals the secret of the mystical sense.
BOOK ONE. THE BLESSING OF JUDAH.

1. He says, then: Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hands [shall be] on the back of your enemies (Gen. 49:8). This can be referred either to Judah himself or to those kings who appear to have descended from him, who, administering the kingdom of that people, subdued the backs of their enemies. But it is also fittingly taken of Christ, who is deservedly praised by his brothers, that is, by the apostles, whom he himself called brothers in the Gospels (Matt. 28). His enemies, on whose backs his hands are, are understood to be those whom the Father promises he will put under his feet, saying, Until I put your enemies under your feet (Ps. 109). They are enemies, then, as long as they are unbelieving and faithless, and therefore they are struck on the back; but after they have been converted they become brothers and praise him who, having called them into adoption by the Father, made them his co-heirs and brothers. And he rightly said that the backs of enemies are struck by Christ: for all who worshipped idols turned their backs to God, as the Lord also reproaches through the prophet, saying: For they have turned their backs to me, and not their face (Jer. 2:27). These backs, then, he strikes, so that, once converted, they may at last turn their backs to idols and lift their face to God, and do what is written in what follows: And the sons of your father shall worship you. For then, when they worship him, they were made sons of the Father and received the spirit of adoption, in which they cry, Abba, Father (Gal. 4). For no one calls Jesus Christ Lord except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12). This statement is referred to Judah somewhat harshly, unless we say it loosely, [meaning] that the sons of Judah were worshipped as kings by their brothers, that is, by their other fellow tribesmen.

2. Judah is a lion's whelp; from the shoot, my son, you have gone up: lying down you slept like a lion, and like a lion's whelp: who shall rouse him? (Gen. 49:9). In these little verses we are no longer merely hemmed in, but almost shut out; for if we explain that Judah can be called a lion's whelp on account of his prowess in war, how shall it be explained that the son is said to have gone up from the shoot? Now 'shoot' here is called βλαστόν in the Greek, which is more properly rendered 'sapling' or 'branch', such as usually sprouts again from the root or from the very trunk of the tree. From what sapling, then, or from what branch will Judah be said to have gone up, or how [will he be said], lying down, to have slept like a lion and like a lion's whelp, so that it is asked who will rouse him? Unless perhaps someone, forcing [the text], should wish to maintain it thus: that Judah came forth from the shoot, that is, as we said above, from a sapling or from a branch, which would signify [his descent] from the very strength and might of his father; and that he, in confidence of his might, lies down and rests like a lion and like a lion's whelp; and that no one would dare to rouse him, since because of the greatness of his forces and the power of the blessed no one would dare to rouse him to battle. But far more fittingly will the mystical exposition be applied to this place, in which the lion's whelp designates Christ, not only naturally but also figuratively. For the Physiologus writes this about the lion's whelp: that when it is born it sleeps for three days and three nights; and that then the roaring or bellowing of its father, as though the place of its lair were shaken, rouses the sleeping whelp. This whelp, then, went up from the shoot: for Christ was born of a Virgin, not of seed, but of a virgin without union with a man and without natural seed, like a sapling or a branch. In this both the reality of the flesh assumed from the Virgin is most plainly declared in the sacred shoot, and it is cleared of the taint of carnal and human seed. Lying down you slept like a lion, and like a lion's whelp. It is plainly shown that he lay down and slept, [the prophet] being about to speak of the suffering of death. But let us see why he sleeps like a lion and like a lion's whelp. Of the whelp's sleep it has already been said above that it is very fittingly applied to Christ, who, buried three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, completed the sleep of death. But 'like a lion' I think should be understood in this way: the death of Christ was the overthrow and triumph over the demons, for all the prey which that adverse lion had seized, when man was laid low and cast down, this lion of ours snatched away: and so, returning from the underworld and ascending on high, he led captivity captive (Eph. 4:8). In this way, then, even in his sleep he was a lion, conquering and vanquishing all things, and he destroyed him who had the power of death (Acts 3). And like a lion's whelp he is roused on the third day. Who shall rouse him? Rightly the saying expresses the person of the prophet as though asking who would rouse Christ, since the Apostle indeed says: That God raised him from the dead. And: He who raised Christ from the dead will also raise your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you (Rom. 8). And again Christ himself says in the Gospels: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up; but he was speaking of the temple of his body (John 2). Since, then, he himself says that he raised his temple, and God is said to have raised him, rightly the Prophet, astonished in amazement at so great a unity and indistinguishability of Father and Son, says: Who shall rouse him?

3. A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until those things come which are laid up (and as is found in other copies, Until he comes for whom it is laid up), and he shall be the expectation of the nations (Gen. 49:10). This place plainly refers to Judah: for it is agreed that until the Nativity of Christ princes did not fail from the race of Judah, nor leaders from his thighs, down to King Herod, who, according to the reliable history which Josephus writes, is said to have been a foreigner and to have crept into the kingdom of the Jews through ambition. As soon, then, as this happened, and the leader failed from the thighs of Judah, he came for whom the kingdom was laid up; and how the nations hope in him, the faith of the Gospel and the spread of the Churches teach. Now those things are said to be 'laid up' which are to be brought forth at the fitting time, just as Christ also is said to have come at the end of the ages, when the Apostle says: Behold, now is the acceptable time (2 Cor. 6), namely for bestowing salvation on the nations. But if anyone wishes to fit the course of both expositions at every point, he can perhaps wrest [the text] so that these things too may seem to be understood of Christ in this way: that a prince shall not fail from Judah, that is, those who after his resurrection are ordained princes of the Churches; and a leader from his thighs: the leaders also of the Christian people, from the thighs of Christ. In this way he will explain that the members of Christ must without doubt be understood spiritually, which the Apostle says are the faithful people (1 Cor. 6). His thighs, then, understood spiritually, can also indicate those who, by the firmness and constancy of their strength, seem to sustain and bear the whole body of the Church; or, since the matter of human seed is customarily spoken of figuratively under the name of the thighs, and among us he who sows sows the word (Luke 8), those who perform the ministry of the word for the Church can be understood as the leaders from Christ's thighs. Until those things come which are laid up for him: it will seem that this can be understood thus, that until the consummation of the age these leaders will not be lacking, until those things come which are laid up, which God has prepared for those who love him. And he shall be the expectation of the nations: that is, on the day of judgement, when all nations and peoples will await Christ as judge in fear of heart and trembling of conscience.

4. Binding his foal to the vine, and the foal of his ass to the branch of the vine (Gen. 49:11). This is said properly and uniquely of Christ: for he bound his foal to the vine who said: I am the true vine (John 15). To this vine, then, he binds both his own foal and the foal of his ass (Mark 11). His foal is the people from the nations, on whom no burden of the Law had ever yet been laid, and on which no one had sat except he himself first (Luke 19). The foal of his ass, however, is those from the former people, who is now named under the figure of the ass, who were chosen for salvation, of whom the Prophet says: Though the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved (Hos. 1). The ass, then, being cast off, which preferred to carry the burden of the Law in unbelief, the foal born of her is chosen; that is, a new people out of the old is taken up through faith and joined to the people from the nations. Christ, then, is called the vine in respect of that part by which he took up human nature, to which the Word of God binds his foal, that is, joins his people and unites them to that way of life which he himself led in the flesh: so that by imitating him the foal which is bound to him may become with him both a son of God and a co-heir (Rom. 8). As for the branch of the vine, whose meaning we explained at the beginning, we can understand it in this way. The faith which is in Christ both holds the rule of the present life and supplies the confidence of future hope. The vine, then, seems to show this: that those who believe in him and cling to him imitate the deeds of Christ while he was in the flesh; but the branch of the vine, that is, the tendril (Greek ἕλιξ), which is understood not so much as the branch as that by which the branch is attached to the tree and secured against falling (made safe by which support, it scorns and repels winds and whirlwinds), indicates the hope of good things to come, since all the faithful await the consummation of salvation not only in what they have done but also in what they hope and believe is to come: in which, bound and secured by hope as if to a kind of tree of patience, they bear the storms and whirlwinds of temptations. To interpret this of the historical Judah no reasoning, it seems to me, can permit, unless, attending to Jewish fables, we think it can be understood according to what they say: that the portion of the tribe of Judah which it received as its inheritance of land was so full of vineyards that, as though no shrub of any other kind existed, the abundance of vines seemed so great that there was not even the possibility of tying an animal to any other kind of tree. But these things, as we said, will seem rather Jewish inventions; let the mystical exposition please us more, even if it stands alone.

5. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape (Gen. 49:11). These words too will seem to belong only to the historical exposition, and to signify a field fertile in vines and, by hyperbole, an abundance of wine; but the mystical exposition brings out a nobler sense. For the robe of Christ which is washed in wine is rightly understood as the Church, which he cleansed for himself with his own blood, having neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. 5). For, says the Apostle, you were not redeemed with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of the Only-begotten of God (1 Pet. 1). In the wine of this blood, then, that is, in the washing of regeneration, the Church is washed by Christ. For we are buried with him through Baptism into his death and blood, that is, we are baptised into his death. But how he washes his cloak in the blood of the grape must be considered. The cloak seems to be a garment nearer to the body, or more hidden, than the robe. Those, then, who, washed earlier through the washing [of Baptism], had been made his robe, after they have come to the sacrament of the blood of the grape, are said to share, as it were, in the inner mystery and in his more hidden cloak. For the soul too is washed in the blood of the grape when it has begun to grasp the meaning of this sacrament. For once the power of the blood, the power of the word of God, has been recognised and understood, the more capacious the soul has been made, the purer it becomes, and it is washed daily for progress in knowledge; and joining itself to the Lord, it will become not only his cloak but now one spirit with him. Contrary to this was that cloak of the people of Israel in which, to signify the shamelessness of the nation, he called it not so much a cloak as a loincloth, which Jeremiah is ordered to put round his loins, and to take off again, and to hide in the Euphrates (Jer. 13).

5. His eyes, it says, are gracious from wine, and his teeth whiter than milk (Gen. 49:12). Do you see how, especially towards the end, it cuts off and severs the historical understanding? For if, arguing still more contentiously, we should wish to say that Judah's eyes are gracious from wine because of the abundance of wine, as we said above, and the abundance of drinking-cups, what shall we answer about white teeth, and the quality of milk brought forward? In this matter one must not act shamelessly against the truth. But, shut out by the breaking-off of the historical understanding, let us return to the order of the spiritual exposition. His eyes, it says, are gracious from wine. We showed above, on the Apostle's authority, that all the worthy among the faithful are called members of Christ, and that they are individually named as different members according to the service each renders to the whole body of the Church. For those will be the feet of Christ who run to make peace, who go to help those placed in need. Those will be the hands of Christ which are stretched out in mercy, which bring help to the needy, which are held out as a support to the weak. So those will be the eyes of Christ who supply the light of knowledge to the whole body, as it is written in the Gospel: The lamp of your body is your eye (Matt. 6:22). These eyes, then, are gracious; for the speech of wisdom is seasoned with salt, so as to give grace to the hearers. It is therefore called gracious not only because it ministers the word of knowledge, but because it produces the grace that it has in itself. For when these things are heard, it says, the wise man will be wiser (Prov. 5). His eyes, then, are gracious from wine, because there is nothing watery in the word of wisdom, nothing fluid, nothing cold, but wine that gladdens the heart of man, and that is poured into the wounds of him who fell among robbers, so that the wounds of the hearers' sins may not only be soothed by the gentleness of oil but also cleansed by the sharpness of wine. And who is it, says the Apostle, who gladdens me, but he who is made sorrowful by me? His teeth are white beyond milk. We have already spoken quite often about the order and meaning of the members of Christ, and to repeat the

same things more frequently in these places seems absurd. His teeth, then, white beyond milk, will be those who can chew the strong and solid food of the word of God and grind it with their teeth to the utmost fineness, of whom the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: But solid food belongs to the perfect, who according to their capacity for taking it have their senses trained to the discernment of good and evil (Heb. 5:14). But of the imperfect Corinthians he says: I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able (1 Cor. 3:2). These things [are] beyond those who are fed on milk: their teeth are white, that is, [beyond] those who cannot take perfect food, and they eat beyond those who, like little children, still need milk. Further, in the Law too we are shown that those animals are clean which chew the cud (Lev. 11) and bring the food they have taken back to the teeth again, and hand it over, finely ground, for the sustenance of the body. Very fittingly indeed he also calls his teeth white. For all who are perfect, and who, explaining the foods of the Scriptures by worthy and fitting interpretations, supply to the body of the Church the fine and minute understanding which is called spiritual, ought to be white and pure and free from every stain, lest perhaps it be said to them: You who teach others, do you not teach yourself? (Rom. 2).

6. But since divine Scripture ought not only to contain knowledge of the sacraments but also to shape the conduct and actions of learners (for so Wisdom too says through Solomon: Write these things for yourself doubly and triply in your heart (Prov. 22); and the ark built by Noah is ordered to be made with two storeys and three storeys (Gen. 6)), let us try, now that we have written these things out doubly, as far as we were able to perceive them, that is, according to the history and according to the mystical understanding, now, as far as the place can admit, to examine the moral sense in it, so that students of the Scriptures may be taught not only what was done in others or by others, but also what they themselves ought to do within themselves. Judah is interpreted 'confession': he, then, who either, confessing his sins, has done penance, or confesses Christ before men in persecution, will be praised by his brothers; for there is gladness and joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15). By them, then, as by brothers (for both men and angels are sons of one Creator and Father), he is praised. But he who confesses the Lord Jesus, since he confesses in the Holy

Spirit, his hands are set upon the backs of his enemies: for he who before had yielded his members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, now yielding them to serve righteousness unto sanctification (Rom. 6), harasses and strikes the backs of his fleeing enemies, that is, the demons. For so he fights, not as one beating the air (2 Cor. 9), but putting demons to flight; and he who, because of very great progress, now has as it were a share of God in himself, is also said to be worshipped by the sons of his father. The sons of his father, as in a moral passage, we can take as the sons of light, who rightly worship and revere those who by knowledge and the merit of works have advanced into the likeness of God. For just as Christ is the light of the world (John 8), so also his disciples are the light of the world (Matt. 5); but he by nature, they by grace. And Moses is said to be the god of Pharaoh (Exod. 7). Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up. Rightly is he called a lion's whelp who has been crucified with Christ and has risen with him, as Paul too said (Rom. 6), who also is rightly taken as Judah, for he confessed his sin, saying: I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor. 15). And again he says that he himself is what Christ is, when he says: I am crucified with Christ; yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me (Gal. 2). He, then, is a lion's whelp who sleeps with Christ while he is dead to sin, and has risen with Christ while he lives to God (Rom. 11). And the son who goes up from a shoot is without doubt he who, though he was a wild olive, was grafted into the [perhaps: good] olive tree, and cast off the rustic and savage ways of carnal nature, an heir through the spirit of adoption (Phil. 4), remaining a true root of life and bearing very much fruit from its graftings. Lying down you slept like a lion. He sleeps like a lion, for the wise man is confident like a lion (Prov. 28), especially when he can say confidently: I can do all things in him who strengthens me (Phil. 4). He is roused by no terrors, no threats, no enticements, but his purpose will remain unmoved and his mind fixed. Nor can a prince ever be lacking from Judah, or a leader from his thighs; for truly he will be able to exercise rule over himself and be a worthy leader who first, through confession and penance, having cut off and subdued all the carnal vices by which he was formerly driven, exercises rule over himself, and does not allow anger, or ambition, or avarice, or lust to exercise rule in him. But he will have a leader from the thighs of Judah, that is, of him who has been amended and corrected by confession, lest, if the blind lead the blind (Matt. 15), that is, if a mind still blinded by vices governs a body blind by nature, both fall into the pit. Until those things come which are laid up for him, as he too said: For the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come which will be revealed in us (Rom. 8). Or certainly each of the saints exercises rule over himself, and will be the leader of his own life, for just so long until that comes to pass that God may be all in all; for this is laid up at the end. And he shall be the expectation of the nations. Since we have once set out to pursue the moral sense, we must also look for these nations within ourselves, which have an expectation. As the nations within us of this man, so amended by confession and perfected, we can understand all the movements of our soul which stir more fiercely in us in our early age and behave, as it were, like Gentiles: for these all hope of amendment and expectation lies in this, that the mind, which is the prince and leader of man, having confessed Christ and been enlightened by him, should steer the helm of its actions. Binding his foal to the vine. By foal here let us understand the mind itself in its renewal of life, which elsewhere is called by the Lord a little child, when he says: Unless you are converted and become like a little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19). When, therefore, someone joins himself to the Lord and becomes one spirit with him, he binds his foal to the vine, saying: But for me it is good to cleave to God (Ps. 72). And the foal of his ass to the branch of the vine. This branch, that is, what we explained above as the tendril (Greek ἕλιξ), we can take as the fine and winding understanding of knowledge, by which the foal of the ass, that is, the disposition of the soul's mind, keeps the soul itself from falling. He shall wash his robe in wine. Just as the flesh of the Word of God is the food of the perfect, so also his blood is the drink of the perfect. Those, then, who are cleansed and renewed day by day through the Word of God are said to wash their robe in wine, that is, their visible actions, and their cloak in the blood of the grape, [that is,] their inner thoughts, as the Apostle too said: Cleansing thoughts, and every height exalting itself against the knowledge of Christ (2 Cor. 10). Yet it can also be understood solely of the glory and suffering of martyrdom, which the righteous man hopes daily to suffer in the flesh, and of the cloak alone in blood. Nonetheless he takes [it as] the martyrdom of conscience, which he endures within himself unceasingly. Then, in what follows, he says that his eyes are gracious from wine, and his teeth white beyond milk. There is no doubt that the praise of the eyes is brought forward on account of their power of looking ahead and seeing far, which certainly comes through either the grace or the study of knowledge. For this reason also the teeth are white, which eat the pure, spotless and solid foods of the word of God, and do not allow the soul to be fed on the milk of little children, but nourish it on solid and strong foods, that is, carrying it over from moral to mystical and doctrinal matters, by which, enlightened, it may with unveiled face behold the glory of the Lord.
PAULINUS
TO BROTHER RUFINUS, greeting.

Our son Cerealis has left me uncertain whether he would reach you at the time when he returns to holy Peter [at Rome]. Yet we judged that not to write to you by one who is as much yours as ours would be as blameworthy for us as it would be saddening to you. And so, preferring to risk the loss of a sheet of paper, if he should perhaps not see you, rather than, as we believe, the loss of a duty, if he should see you, we have entrusted this letter not to chance but to faith. For we believe in the Lord that the way of our letter and of our son will be directed to you, since for those who desire the good all things will turn out for good: for he desires you as much as you ought to be desired by one who understands what he gains from fellowship with you. And so I presume that, in accordance with his faith and piety, his desire will be kept safe among good things, and he will reach you and remain with you; and a saving protection will be doubled for us before the Lord in you both, when so good a son has joined you as companion and as disciple and helper, and you, given to him by the Lord as father and teacher of all good, have added the strength of spiritual grace to the effective power of [his] prayers. As for us, although your love lets us presume that, when you are about to return to the East, you will not bear to go away without visiting us, yet because of our sins there is fear that, even though so near to us, the daughter of Babylon may turn you aside. Therefore we commend our desires and prayers to the Lord, that he may act toward us not according to our merit but according to our desire, and direct your way to us in the way of his peace; for those who do not walk in it are condemned to a reprobate mind, and do not deserve to desire you.

2. Indeed, with the importunity with which I am accustomed to knock at your door even at midnight, or rather, driven back by fear and forced into modesty and moderation in asking, I now hand over to you this task concerning me: that the Blessings of the twelve Patriarchs, whose beginning you have already published for me in written pages, expounding the prophecy concerning the person of Judah in a threefold interpretation, as was requested, you would deign to expound as they are distributed among the remaining sons. So may I myself through you come to know the truth, and have [you as] the source of great thanks and praise, if to those who, thinking more of me than I deserve, have judged that I should be consulted about the work, I reply with divine things from your spirit rather than with foolish things from my own mind.
PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCHS, BY RUFINUS OF AQUILEIA, PRESBYTER, TO PAULINUS, PRESBYTER.
RUFINUS TO BROTHER PAULINUS,
MAN OF GOD, greeting.

I had not yet seen our common son Cerealis, but he, aware what pain he would inflict on me if he delayed delivering your letter, sent it ahead to me. As I read it, growing (as I usually do) more and more in my longing for you, I found at the end that you command the very thing for which I have often excused myself to you, namely that you should not ask me to answer anything by letter about the interpretation of the Scriptures; and so that you would the more readily stop asking, I gave you once and again proof of my lack of skill and of my unlearned speech.

2. But since even so you do not weary of commanding, I have, as I could even now, added [an account] of the remaining eleven Patriarchs to what I had earlier answered you about the blessing of Judah, thinking that I have done the will of that father to whom, when he bade me go into the vineyard, I said, I am not going (Matt. 15), and afterwards went. If there is indeed any rashness in the deed, in that we, though less than competent, touch such great matters, it will (by your leave I say it) most justly be reckoned to you, who out of excessive love do not see that the measures of knowledge in us, as of the other virtues, are quite

short. And since I wrote this back to you during the days of Lent, while staying in the monastery of Pinetum, I could not hide my follies even from the brothers who were present; and they too, thinking it something great that can please you, nonetheless wrung from me permission to copy these things for themselves. So, even when you ask me for your food, you also give drink to others. Farewell in peace, most beloved brother, truest worshipper of God, and Israelite in whom there is no guile; and be mindful of me, man of God full of grace.
BOOK TWO.
ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE REMAINING ELEVEN PATRIARCHS.

It must first be understood that in each of the places where Scripture mentions the twelve Patriarchs there is great diversity in the very order in which they are written. One order is written at their birth (Gen. 35); another when they are related to enter the land of Egypt together with their father Israel and the offspring of their posterity (Gen. 46); another now, when they receive the blessings of their dying parent (Gen. 49); another when, as tribes that have come out of Egypt, they are recorded as doing something in the desert (Exod. 14 and following), or when, having entered the land of promise, they are stationed on Mount Gerizim and on Mount Ebal for the blessings and curses (Deut. 27). Another again when they receive by lot the division of the land of inheritance (Josh. 15). And this order varies so much that at times some of them are not even found entered in the number. It is certain that this does not vary without some reason, and that there are probable causes why in one place one is preferred, and in another another is put first. But you, [Brother Paulinus,] have not now set these matters before us, but only that we should explain, as God grants, what is contained in the blessings which they receive from their father at the time of his death. These may perhaps be called Blessings solely because it is said at the end: And their father spoke these things to them, and blessed them; he blessed them each according to his own blessing (Gen. 49:28). Otherwise, at the beginning, where the father calls them together, he does not call them as if to a blessing, but it is written thus: And Jacob called his sons, and said: Gather together, that I may announce to you what will befall you in the last days (ibid. 2); which certainly signifies rather a prophecy, by which what will happen to them is foretold. Yet in the bodily sequence of the words itself there are neither blessings only nor solely a foretelling of the future, but also [rebuke] by which either the conduct or the intention of them, or even certain deeds done by them, are notably censured. This matter supplies us with a threefold material for explanation, as we did in the other case too, so that the blessings keep the place of the history, the prophecy that of the mystical and doctrinal [sense], while the correction and rebuke of conduct directs the pen of the moral [sense].
THE BLESSING OF REUBEN.

1. Reuben (he says), my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sons, hard in conduct, and hard [and] rash: you have heaped insults, like water you shall not boil over. For you went up onto your father's bed; then you defiled the couch where you went up (Gen. 49:3-4). The story of the incest is hidden from no one: how Reuben burned with the flame of lust for his father's concubine and stained his father's couch (Gen. 34). But that at the beginning he seems to ascribe something of praise to him, saying, You are my strength, is so that he may be marked more heavily in his crime, who, though he was held to be his father's strength and the beginning of his sons, did not know how to keep reverence toward his father; like that which is said through the Prophet: I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly fertile; how have you turned into bitterness, a foreign vine? (Jer. 2).

2. According to the mystical understanding, however, it seems to me that Reuben can bear the person of the former people, the Jews, who are both firstborn and the beginning of the sons, as the Prophet also says: Israel is my firstborn (Exod. 4). For to them first were given the oracles of God. And that this people was hard and rash the Scriptures declare; for the Prophet says of them: Everything that this people speaks is hard (Isa. 8). And again elsewhere it says of them: You are always stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart (Acts 7). It heaped injuries on God the Father when it turned its back to him and not its face (Jer. 2). And it defiled the couch of the concubine which it went up onto, that is, the law of the Old Testament, which it often stained by transgressing. That the law of the Old Testament is represented in the person of a concubine Paul taught, saying: Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman; and these are the Testaments (Gal. 4); in which Hagar, who was a concubine, is placed as a type of the Old Testament. For there was one perfect dove and mother, who, a chaste virgin, a queen to the bridegroom king, the Church, is joined to Christ through the Gospel.

3. But the moral [sense] of this passage will also be treated by us thus. Reuben is interpreted by the elders as "son who is seen," that is, visible and fleshly: he is, I believe, the one of whom the Apostle says, The first man was from the earth, earthly (1 Cor. 15). And also elsewhere: For if our man who is seen is being corrupted, yet the one who is within is being renewed (2 Cor. 4). This same one who is seen he calls the outer man. And again he says: For what is spiritual is not first, but what is animal is first (1 Cor. 15). So every man, while he lives in a fleshly way in this world and is moved according to the flesh — and the first fleshly movement is in the desire of lust, which the time of early youth soon obeys — [this movement] renders the man hard and rash and at the same time wanton, going up even onto his father's bed and defiling his father's couch, that is, transgressing even the precepts and warnings of the natural law which is in us (which is here called the father's couch). For there is within us a certain natural law, which reproves each person who sins and suggests to him that what he does wrong is evil. So he violates the bed of this Law and stains the seat of its privacy who is carried headlong and unbridled into vices.
THE BLESSING OF SIMEON AND LEVI.

1. Simeon and Levi, brothers, accomplished the iniquity of their will. Into their council let my soul not enter, and in their council let my inward parts not be invited (Gen. 49:5-6). As far as the history is concerned, he seems to blame that deed of theirs, that by fraud and deceit they slaughtered Hamor and his son Shechem, who after lying with their sister had wished to be joined to the family of Israel, and killed all his people, when their father Israel also said to them: You have made me hateful in this world (Gen. 34). So he calls down a curse on their fury for its rashness, and declares that they are to be divided among the peoples of Israel, inasmuch as from them would come the Levites and priests, who had no allotted share in the land of promise.

2. A spiritual explanation of these [words], however, seems to me able to be fitted thus: that Simeon and Levi can bear the persons of the scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people, of whom it is written: The scribes and Pharisees held a council to seize Jesus by guile (Matt. 26). Of this council the holy man, who saw God with his mind, now says: Into their council let my soul not enter; and in their council, in which, having brought in false witnesses, they condemned Jesus, let my inward parts not, he says, be invited. Does he not seem to you to be saying this: I am clean of the blood of this just man (Matt. 27); I am clean of the sentence that you decree against an innocent man? For in their anger, he says, they killed men. I ask what men they killed, since it is certain that before the Lord's passion none of the believers was punished: unless perhaps someone also ascribes to them the blood of the Prophets. For the Lord also says to them that from the blood of Abel the just up to the blood of Zechariah (Matt. 23), all the blood of the just that has been shed shall be required of that very generation. But let us see whether perhaps they also killed those men whom they persuaded to cry out, His blood be on us and on our children (Matt. 27). And in their desire they hamstrung a bull. That the Son of God is called a bull we read in the figures of the Scriptures, namely in the Gospel, where it is written in the person of the elder son saying to his father: I have always been with you and have never transgressed your command, and you never gave me a kid, that I might feast with my friends; but when this younger son of yours came, who squandered all his substance, you killed for him this fatted calf (Luke 15). So the scribes and Pharisees are said to have hamstrung by their council the bull or calf; and their fury is cursed because it is rash, and their anger because it is hardened. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel. We must see whether perhaps this division mentioned here is such as the one of which it is said in the Gospel: When the master of that servant comes, he will divide him and put his portion with the unbelievers (Luke 12). Or certainly, as I heard one of the holy fathers explaining, division and scattering are both named because some of them believed in the Lord and others remained in unbelief. Those are said to be divided who are separated from them and come to faith; and those scattered whose unbelieving race, their homeland and temple overthrown, is scattered throughout the world.

3. The moral figure, however, can perhaps be kept thus. Many wise men have held that the power of the soul is threefold, that is, that there are three kinds of its movement: through anger, through desire, through reason; nor, I think, can any other movement of the soul be found besides these. For everything by which it strives or is moved belongs either to anger, or to desire, or to reason; and therefore the whole state of human life seems to me to be foreshadowed in these three sons of Jacob, and through them this threefold movement of the soul to be signified. Among them Reuben keeps the first kind, that of desire, into which he is marked with a stain as having poured himself out. Simeon holds the second kind, that of anger or fury, which is itself shown by the reproach of his fury. Levi holds the third form, that of rational movement, since to him was entrusted also the keeping of the law. These three kinds, then, almost every soul that comes into this world seems to me to exercise culpably in its first movements, until, weighed down by the vices of sins and wearied by a surfeit of evils, it can come to the place of penitence. For Judah follows after this, to purge sins by confession, since Judah in the Hebrew tongue is interpreted confession, which is said to free from death. Concerning Judah, I believe what we have already said earlier, as best we could, is sufficient; and if it pleases, it can either be joined to these [remarks] or set before them.
THE BLESSING OF ZEBULUN.

1. Zebulun shall dwell by the sea, and he is a landing-place for ships, and he extends as far as Sidon (Gen. 49:13). The history indicates the portion and lot of the future inheritance. As for the mystery, we read in the Gospel that some of the Apostles were taken from these regions, and that the Lord often taught in these very places, as it is written: Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles: the people that sat in darkness has seen a great light (Isa. 9; Matt. 4). But as to his saying, And he extends as far as Sidon: Sidon is interpreted hunter, or huntress. And whom else shall we take to be meant in a praiseworthy sense by hunters in this place, if not the Apostles of the Lord, of whom the prophet foretold: For I will send many hunters, and they will hunt them on every mountain (Jer. 16)?

2. If, however, a moral sense is sought here too, Zebulun is interpreted nocturnal flowing. So it may seem to follow that after the soul which sat in darkness has seen the light of the Lord, and has turned to penitence from confession, all those things which it had done in the death of ignorance are taken away from it and flow off; and after confession has gone before in Judah, conversion also follows in this one, when everything that belonged to night and darkness now flows away, in which it tries as it were to strip off the old man and to lay aside the things of the night, so that it may walk honestly as in the day (Rom. 13). But this, that he stretches himself out as far as Sidon, that is, as far as the hunters, perhaps declares that he too now strives to be one of those to whom it is said: Catch for me the little foxes that destroy my vineyards (Song 2). Therefore he extends himself as far as the hunters, so that he may himself learn to hunt, if ever any wild beasts or crafty foxes — that is, either savage demons or harmful thoughts — creep into his heart and wish to destroy the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth: so that he may seize them, having become a praiseworthy hunter of evil thoughts.
THE BLESSING OF ISSACHAR.

1. Issachar desired the good; he shall rest in the midst of the lots, seeing the rest, that it is good, and the land, that it is rich. Here too the order of the history is fittingly kept, in that he dwelt in the midst of the lots, that is, in the divisions of the land which was distributed to them by Joshua son of Nun (Josh. 19). For in the book of Joshua son of Nun himself the fourth lot of the latter seven tribes is reported to have come out; for two tribes, that is, Judah and Ephraim, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had received [theirs] earlier. And Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh had their possession beyond the Jordan. So Issachar is in the middle, since he is the fourth of seven: a farmer of rich and fertile soil, willingly spending labour on fertile ground. And let this be said as far as the history is concerned.

2. But Issachar, since [the name] is interpreted 'reward', can stand as a figure of those who say: For if I preach willingly, I have a reward (1 Cor. 9). And of whom it is said: Behold, the inheritance of the Lord [is] sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb (Ps. 126). For the Apostles are rightly to be thought the reward of the Son of God, because he deigned to enter the Virgin's womb. For they are the ones who desired the good, of whose souls it is said in the Song of Songs: The young maidens have loved you (Song 1); and who say to Jesus: We will run after you, into the fragrance of your ointments (ibid.). Resting in the midst of the lots, that is, in the midst of the good land, the land flowing with milk and honey: in the midst of it they rest. This land flowing with milk and honey was Jesus, on whose breast not only John (John 13) but, in John, all the disciples reclined; and they became farmers. That these were farmers, and cultivated our land, which they had seen to be rich and good, and which the Son of Man had come to sow, and his seed fell on good land (Matt. 13), which would bear fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold (Luke 8) — of this all Scripture bears witness, and especially the Apostle Paul, who says: For it is God's management, it is God's cultivation (1 Cor. 3). And again the same [Apostle] says: The farmer who labours ought to be the first to receive of the fruits (2 Tim. 2). And again he says of himself: Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit (1 Cor. 9)? But perhaps you say: And how is it true that the Apostles saw rest, as is said here, And seeing the rest, that it is good, when it is agreed that the Apostles never had rest, but spent the whole time of their life in labours and in persecutions, as the Apostle Paul indicates (2 Cor. 11)? Let us see, then, whether this is not what this saying means, when it says, And seeing the rest, that it is good: that, considering the future rest, and beholding the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven and the glory of all that has been promised, they willingly put their shoulders to the labour. For looking to those good things which are to come, they patiently bore present evils, just as the Apostle Paul also says of Moses, that, scorning the treasures of the Egyptians, he chose rather to bear the reproach of Christ: For he looked, he says, to the reward (Heb. 11).

3. But since we have undertaken to build the ark of divine Scripture not only with two storeys but with three (as was said to Noah by the Lord, Gen. 6), let us now see how Issachar builds for us a third nest as well. Above we took up that man who [was] wandering through the threefold movement of the soul (as is the sickness of the whole soul), in anger and fury, which we distinguished as able to be signified by Reuben through desire, by Simeon through anger, and by Levi through prudence not rightly directed. But we have shown him now penitent in Judah, and in Zebulun converted in great part, and in Issachar, which is interpreted 'reward', we now see him also awaiting the reward of good work, since he has not only cast off evil but also desired the good, and he rests in the midst of the lots. Now he is in the middle who, according to the admonition of Wisdom, turns aside neither to the right nor to the left; for this is to keep the line straight and to walk the way of virtue. In this the lots too can be understood thus. A lot is that by which a portion of the inheritance is assigned to each, not one which seems to depend on some chance, as the Gentiles think, but one which is decided by the judgement and dispensation of God. So in this moral exposition the lots are to be understood by us as the commandments of God, through which the heavenly inheritance will be obtained. This man, then, who is now converted and also hopes for the reward of his works, always rests in the midst of the lots, that is, in the midst of the commandments of God, seeing the rest, that it is good, and the land, that it is rich. After he had driven off and shut out the battle of thoughts that was within him, while in him the flesh lusted against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, his spirit rested in God; and then he saw that rest is good, when Jesus could now say to him: Come aside a little, and rest. But he also saw the land, that it is good. When did he see the good land? When he purged his flesh of vices and lusts, then he saw that it was beyond doubt good and rich land, which bears the fruits of righteousness in good works. For seeing this, he put his shoulder to labouring, and became a farmer. He is to be thought a farmer of his own land who unceasingly cleaves and furrows the fields of his soul and the fallow ground of his heart with the plough of the word of God and the ploughshare of the Scriptures, who waters the plantings of faith and charity, of hope and righteousness, from the fountains of Israel, and who discovers the whole discipline of agriculture in the countryside of his own soul.
THE BLESSING OF DAN.

1. Dan shall judge his people as though one tribe in Israel. And let Dan be a serpent in the way, sitting on the path, biting the horse's heel, and the rider shall fall backward. Awaiting salvation from the Lord. Since the history of this passage is not, so far as the smallness of my understanding reaches, easily found clearly expressed in the holy Scriptures — either how Dan judged the people as one tribe, or how he sat in the way — lest we perhaps put forward something that seems to have too little proof from the Scriptures, it seems to me that what is written should rather be applied to a spiritual understanding. Unless perhaps these written words are to be compared with some deeds done in those wars which are related as written either by Joshua son of Nun or in the book of Judges. Although, searching rather carefully, we have not yet found anything that would satisfy our purpose, we nevertheless set out what is held in the opinion of some.

2. Some say that by these words the Antichrist is foretold as going to come from this tribe; others suspect that these things were written about Judas the traitor, and want the rider and the horse to signify the Lord with the flesh he took up. But such an understanding seems to me hardly able to be explained: for even if they wish to place the Godhead in the horse, it certainly could not be bitten by a serpent; if in the rider, it would not fittingly be said of the Godhead of the Word that it falls backward and awaits salvation from the Lord. Hence I think that Dan is perhaps more rightly applied to him who is awaited as judge of the living and the dead, since Dan is interpreted 'judgement' or 'judge'. So the Lord Jesus Christ, who says: I came into this world for judgement (John 9); and again: The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son (ibid. 5) — he himself will judge his people as one tribe. For there will no longer be a division of tribes, nor any difference, but, as he himself says: There will be one flock and one shepherd (ibid. 10).

3. But what seems to deter some in this passage is the saying that follows: Let Dan be a serpent in the way. And because the serpent is frequently set in the Scriptures for the person of the devil, they think this cannot suit the Lord. But if we return to the Scriptures: just as we find the devil called a lion, who goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5), and the opposing powers called bulls, as there: Fat bulls surrounded me (Ps. 21); and again Judah, expounded to us a little earlier, taught that the Lord too is called a lion; we also find the Lord himself called a bull, the one who was slain for the salvation and return of the penitent son (Luke 15). And there are many other similar things in the Scriptures which are drawn now to a good sense, now to a bad one. So too the serpent is found sometimes written even for the person of the Lord, as he himself says of himself in the Gospels: For just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up (John 3). And the Apostle too, when he enjoins [us] to become wise as serpents, did he not apply the name of serpent in a good sense? So in this passage too it can be said of the Lord himself: Let Dan be a serpent in the way, sitting on the path; that is, he who judges hearts and knows what is hidden within, seeing in the way, that is, in the course of this life, riders riding on a road that is not straight. Now the riders can be understood as souls placed in bodies, as it says there: All who mounted horses have slumbered (Ps. 75), that is, all who are in bodies have sinned, as the Apostle also declared. So this serpent, sitting by the way, bites the heel of these horses or riders; and he bites the heel when he wears down the body with sicknesses or with any other torments, so as to check the swift course of sinners. For when the body is afflicted and the flesh consumed, then the rider falls backward; that is, the soul that was riding badly and hastening to perdition falls backward and is called back to patience [perhaps 'penitence'], so that, hindered from its evil course, it may be called back and come to be behind him who says: Come after me (Mark 1). I think something of this sort was also done in the case of the Apostle Peter, when, as the Lord was saying that the Son of Man must be crucified and die (Matt. 16), he himself said: Be merciful, Lord, this shall not happen to you. In this, since out of excessive love he was riding wrongly through ignorance, in the end he is bitten by the Lord as by a serpent, in that it is said to him: Get behind me, Satan, you are a stumbling block to me, for you do not savour the things of God but those of men (Mark 8). And so Peter, called back, awaits salvation from the Lord through the cross and resurrection, which, riding and running too hotly then, he did not know in his ignorance would come. These things moved me in this passage; yet I do not exclude the opinion of those who may have been able to prove what they think by the authority of the Scriptures.

3. But so that not even the third sense may pass us by, the man whom we said long ago, in Issachar, had made progress and rested in the commandments, and had become the farmer of his own soul, can be seen now to progress further in Dan as well: he has received the understanding to discern and judge his people, that is, the thoughts of his heart, as one tribe in Israel, that is, to call everything back into unity and concord, so that there is in him no disagreement of thoughts or counsels. He also becomes a serpent, according to the Lord's command which we mentioned a little before, Be wise as serpents (Matt. 10); yet he sits in the way, and never departs from the path. For a path is understood as a narrower way, which shows that he does not walk along that broad and spacious [way] which leads to death, but along the narrow and strait one which leads to life (Matt. 7). And he bites the horse's heel, doing what the Apostle Paul says: For I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate (1 Cor. 9). And he does this so that the horse may fall backward. For such a man always fears exaltations and heights, and wishes his soul to fall from an evil height to a good humility, so that he may learn from Jesus, because he is humble and meek of heart (Matt. 11). For it is proper to those who are progressing to fear exaltation. Indeed, even so great and so worthy an Apostle as Paul said: Lest I be exalted, a goad was given to my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me (2 Cor. 12). So, then, he calls his soul back from the height, and it, brought back behind the humility of Christ, awaits salvation from the Lord.
THE BLESSING OF GAD.

1. A band of pirates shall try him, but he shall try them at their heels. As history, we do not easily find anything of the sort related in the Scriptures, unless perhaps someone wishes, as it were, to force it and say that, since this tribe obtained its inheritance beyond the Jordan in the parts of Arabia, and since wars of brigands frequently arise there and they meet in constant clashes with one another, these contests of theirs with one another, as if in the manner of pirates, are signified in these words.

2. But truer is the spiritual understanding, which can point to that contest which our Lord and Saviour, placed in the flesh, had against the devil. Now the dwelling of this tribe is near the desert; and Gad is interpreted 'trials'. So that can be

understood which [tells how] the Lord Jesus Christ was led into the desert by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil (Matt. 4). But see how great mysteries are contained in the Patriarch's words. Gad, he says, a band of pirates shall try him. Let us suppose, as we said, that the person of the Lord is in Gad: him the band of pirates shall try. A band of pirates (piraterium) means a certain troop and conspiracy of pirates. For it is certain that the devil, coming to tempt the Lord, had not come without his ministers and attendants; for just as angels were present with the Lord watching his contest (those of whom the Gospel says after the temptation (ibid.), And angels came and ministered to him), so too his angels were present with the devil, for whom with him Gehenna has been prepared, as the Lord says: Go into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels (ibid. 25). And the saints too, when they fight in the contest, are said to be made a spectacle to this world, both to angels and to men (1 Cor. 4). So the conspiracy of tempters was trying the Lord when [the devil] said to him: If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread (Matt. 4). By these things, then, the devil was trying the Lord. But let us see what this is that he says: But he shall try them at their heels. How did the Lord try those who tried him? If at the first temptation the Saviour had declared to the devil that he was the Son of God, it is certain that he would not have dared to approach a second time to tempt [him]; but now see how he who tempts is himself tempted. For the Lord is in the desert forty days and forty nights; afterwards he was hungry. For if he had not been hungry, the tempter would have recognised the Son of God; but now he hungers, so that, by the Lord showing in himself the frailty of the flesh, he who tempts may himself be tempted, and may approach again as if to tempt a man. So, then, the tempters come to the Lord. But he shall try them at their heels, that is, by the same steps by which the devil had approached to tempt him, he [himself] tempts [him].

3. The moral sense, then, is discussed in a similar way: for that man of ours, repenting after confessing his error, rendered [himself] converted through understanding, and has progressed somewhat, so that after progress he comes to this, that he is tempted by the enemy, and the strength of his mind and the constancy of his purpose are proved: for so Scripture says, He who has not been tempted is not proven (Eccl. 34). Nor will anyone at any time at all arrive at perfection, unless he has first given proofs [perhaps 'of himself'] in his temptations.
THE BLESSING OF ASHER.

1. Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall give food to princes. I believe the champions of the letter understand in these words that his region and inheritance of land was fertile and rich, so that it supplied even royal needs. But some of ours think it was said also on account of Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who is related in the Gospels to have been the first, with Simeon, to prophesy about the Lord (Luke 2), and by the faith of her prophecy to have given, as it were, food to princes, that is, to the Apostles and the other believers, namely the things that had been prophesied about him.

2. But since Asher is interpreted 'blessed', of that man whom, called back from error through penitence, we are now leading little by little through each step up to the increases of blessedness — after conversion, after spiritual understanding, after victory over temptations — his bread is said to be rich. For he eats that bread which came down from heaven (John 1) and gives life to this world, and that bread is rich.

3. What he says, rich bread, we can understand thus. Those who understand nothing more in Christ than Christ Jesus and him crucified also eat bread from heaven, but dry and meagre; but those who are worthy to have the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of Christ revealed to them (Col. 2) are those for whom the bread is rich, as it was for Paul, who said: I know both how to abound and how to hunger; in all things and among all I have been instructed (Phil. 4). For if our Lord and Saviour, when he deigns to assume the figure of a bull, is said to be slaughtered for the penitent son as a fat and fatted bull (Luke 15), why should not those who arrive at blessedness in the same way be said to have rich bread? And such a man, for whom the bread is now rich, will also give food to princes. What kind of food? Without doubt [that] of the word of God; and he will give food not to any poor people or recipients whatever, but he will give it to princes: for he too will speak wisdom among the perfect (1 Cor. 2).
THE BLESSING OF NAPHTALI.

1. A tree let loose (or, as our copies have it, a vine spread wide), bringing forth beauty in its fruits. The history signifies that Gad, earlier, received the lot of inheritance in the fertility of the plains, and after him Naphtali possessed country fruitful in shrubs and wooded with trees.

2. But in the mystical exposition, already in the earlier [part] too, when we were discussing Zebulun, we also said what seemed [right] to us about the name of Naphtali, as it is joined with him in the Gospels: that is, that the root and origin, as it were, of the blessed Apostles came forth from their places and region, and that the peoples of those who sat in darkness saw a great light. And the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali (Ps. 67), who are proclaimed through David, are certainly referred to the person of the Apostles.

3. As regards the third explanation, the interpretation of the name Naphtali is this very thing which his father now expresses in blessing him: that is, either 'a tree spread wide' or 'a vine'. So that man of ours, who a little before was feeding on rich bread and from it was giving food to princes (the bread which strengthens the heart of man (Ps. 103)), now in consequence the true vine, Christ, has also brought forth for him beautiful fruit, so that the heart which he had strengthened with bread he may now gladden with wine; and in both of these he seems to me to have come to such progress that he even receives the sacraments of the priesthood. But if we prefer to understand a tree rather than a vine spread wide, which brings forth beauty in its fruits, what other tree will there be that brings forth beauty in its fruits than the wisdom of God, of which Solomon says: She is a tree of life to those who embrace her (Prov. 3)?
THE BLESSING OF JOSEPH.

1. Joseph is a son increased: a son increased. In the blessing of Joseph even the very surface of the letter is in flower, for he is rightly called a son increased whom the Lord, for the sake of preserving his family, had raised to the second rank in the kingdom. Understand him, then, as increased in wisdom, counsel, constancy, chastity, honour, kingship, virtue, and, what is the summit of all the virtues, in piety; in all these Joseph is rightly said to have been enlarged and increased. When he said, My son [is] envied, he seems to have described him not as one who envies but as one who has suffered envy: that is, one whose glory is so great that it draws envy. This, then, is what he says: My envied son, the younger, return to me: my son not so much by birth as by merits. It seems to me, certainly, not idly set down that the patriarch names Joseph his son three times over, saying: Joseph is a son increased, and a son increased; envied, and my younger son. What does it mean that Joseph alone among all the brothers is named son three times? For my part, by the smallness of my understanding, I take it that Joseph was born to him as a son once (Gen. 30), when he was born of Rachel after she had despaired of having offspring. A second time a son is, as it were, born to him again, when after he had been persuaded of his death he is told that he is alive (ibid. 45). A third time he becomes his son when, by teaching and learning and all those virtues by which he himself saw God, educating and instructing him, he had begotten him as a son in the spirit too. Otherwise it will not fit him that he is called the younger son, since he has Benjamin after him, unless he is felt to be younger in his father's teachings. Return to me, he says. That is, turn your mind to me, so that you may carefully note and inscribe in your heart what is said: you, son Joseph, against whom they took counsel and cursed, and the lords of the bows laid snares for you (ibid. 42). For this too is related by holy Scripture, that his brothers at that time took counsel to kill him, but Judah intervened and checked the murderous plan. When he said, They cursed, this is what they said: Behold, the dreamer comes (ibid.). By the lords of the bows he means men of war; and that their arms were loosened and their bows broken signifies that the undertaking was frustrated through the hand of the mighty one of Jacob, that is, the God of Jacob. From there, he who strengthened Israel, from the God of your father, and my God helped you. Help came to you from the same source from which Israel your father was also strengthened, then without doubt when he wrestled on the way (ibid. 32), and God helped him and gave him the name Israel (ibid. 33). So this same God of mine also blessed you, With the blessing of heaven from on high, and the blessing of the earth. The blessing of heaven signifies wisdom; that of the earth, kingship and power. Because of the blessing of the breasts and the womb, the blessing of your father and your mother. He himself explained what the blessing of the breasts and womb is, by naming the mother, because he obtained not only the paternal but also the maternal blessings. This blessing of father and mother prevailed, he says, In the blessings of the abiding mountains, and in the blessings of the everlasting hills. It may perhaps seem to have been said, of abiding mountains and everlasting hills, because of the immovability of the grace that would abide in him, compared as it is to things that are certainly immovable and lasting. These blessings will be everlasting, he says, Upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the brothers over whom he was set. At the end of the saying he seems to have extended the blessings to the whole number of the brothers, so that the blessings are principally upon the head of Joseph, but through Joseph himself they come also upon those whose leader and master he was.

2. This is what we have understood according to the letter; but if we wish to search out something deeper in this too, Joseph can perhaps be referred to the person of the Lord: so that, just as Joseph, after he was thought dead, is found not only living but even set in kingship, and is for this reason called increased, so also the Lord and Saviour, who among the Jews was thought dead, is found living and reigning in the hearts of the faithful. So our Saviour too was increased after death.
