For before he died, Judaea alone was where God was known (Ps. 75), and in Israel alone was his name great; but after he died out of weakness and rose from the dead out of power (1 Cor. 13), in every land a sacrifice is offered to his name. The Son of God is also called envied; and who bore envy as he did? Of him it is also written: For Pilate knew that the Jews had handed him over out of envy (Matt. 27; Mark 15). The younger son according to the flesh is he who is the last Adam. And what we marked in the historical exposition, the title of son repeated three times, we find much more clearly in this exposition. For he is son before the ages, of whom the Father said: From the womb before the morning star I begot you (Ps. 106). And again son, when he was born of Mary, and it is said through the angel: The holy one that will be born of you will be called the Son of God (Luke 1). And he becomes son a third time when the firstborn rises from the dead, to whom the Father's voice fittingly applies, saying: My younger son, return to me: after you have risen from the dead, ascend as victor into heaven to me too, from whom you set out. Against whom they took counsel, he says, and cursed (Matt. 26): for the scribes and Pharisees had taken counsel to seize Jesus by guile; and they cursed, without doubt, when they said: You are a Samaritan, you have a demon (John 8). The lords of the bows laid snares for him, and their bows were broken with might, and the sinews of the arms of their hands were loosened. The lords of the bows who lay in wait are understood as those who came to him with feigned questions to catch him in his speech, and said to him: Tell us, is it lawful to pay tax to Caesar, or not (Matt. 22)? Bringing out these words, then, like arrows from the bow of their mouth, they aimed them at Jesus, so that if he had said it was not lawful to pay tax to Caesar he would become guilty before Caesar, but if he had said it should be paid he would seem to undo the law. But when he, as the very wisdom of God, having looked at the inscription on the denarius, answered: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's, the sinews of their arms were loosened through the hand of the mighty one of Jacob. That contest of his can also be understood which he had in the desert, when he was tempted by the devil, who aimed at him the arrows of evil suggestions; driving these off with his answers, he loosened the arms and sinews of those who aimed them. From there, he who strengthened Israel, from the God of your father, and helped you. For the Saviour too is said to have been helped by God according to [his] humanity; indeed it is written in the Gospel: When he was sweating in prayer, an angel, it says, came and strengthened him (Luke 22). The exposition may perhaps seem harsher in this place, because what was said above we were taking as said, as it were, in the person of the Father to the Son. But here it is written, And my God helped you and blessed you: how would this fit the person of the Father? But let us see whether perhaps, just as nothing is troubling if the Father says of the Son, because the Son is wisdom, that he is my wisdom; and because the Son is power, it is not absurd if the Father says of him that he is my power; and because the Son is truth, it is not discordant if the Father says, he is my truth; so also, because the Son is God, it may not seem absurd if he says, he is my God: just as it is not called absurd either that the Son says of the Father, For I go to my God and to your God. And he blessed you, he says, with the blessing of heaven from on high, and the blessing of the earth that holds all things (Job 14). That the blessing of heaven is in Christ will not seem unfitting, according to what is said: For the second man is the heavenly one from heaven (1 Cor. 15). But as for the earth, that he said the blessing of the earth that holds all things, because of the blessing of the breasts and womb, it seems to me quite wonderful and great how that earth which is blessed in the Son of God holds all things. I think this is to be understood in this way: each one receives the grace of the Spirit according to the measure of his faith. For to one, according to the measure of faith, is given the word of understanding, to another the word of wisdom, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues (ibid. 12). These you will find one by one in individuals, or at times two or three together; but in that earth, that is, in that flesh which was blessed in Jesus, not only were all these present, but they dwelt there fully and substantially, as the Apostle too says: In whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Because of the blessing of the breasts and the womb (Col. 2). A certain [woman] is also related in the Gospel to have cried out this, without doubt mindful of these words, and to have said: Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked (Luke 11). And that [saying], Because of the blessing, he says, of your father and your mother: of the heavenly Father, who gave the blessing, and of the virgin mother, who received it. It prevailed in the blessings of the abiding mountains. This blessing, he says, which was given to you from highest heaven and from the earth, prevailed over the blessings of the abiding mountains and the blessings of the everlasting hills. Who will the abiding mountains be, if not those to whom Jesus says: You are those who have remained with me in my trials (ibid. 22)? Rightly, then, the Apostles are called abiding mountains, because they remained to the end, and they will be saved. And the everlasting hills: whom else do we understand but those who are ranked by their merits in the second grade after the Apostles, and who attain eternal life? For these will much more truly be believed everlasting than mountains and hills, which perish together with the world. And all these blessings will be upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the brothers over whom he was set. Fittingly all these blessings are said to be placed upon the head of Christ, so that from his head they may come also to the crown of those over whom he is set. Nor is there any other reason why, born in the flesh, he received all these blessings, except that, having them poured into himself from the Father as through a kind of vine-layer, he might himself in turn pour them on to believers; and that, having become mediator between God and men, human nature might receive, through his mediation, foretasting and transfusing them, the blessings which on account of its weakness it could not of itself receive, as he himself also said: For I sanctify myself for them (John 17).

3. But now that man of ours who, in the third sense, restored by spiritual steps, has risen with increasing growth as far as Joseph; who through progress in faith and through the gifts of the Holy Spirit has shone out so greatly that he grew even to the point of [arousing] envy: with what flowers of words shall he be crowned by us, for whom, having fought so good a fight, finished the course, kept the faith, God the just judge prepares the crown of righteousness laid up [for him] (2 Tim. 4)? Of him, then, the father says: Joseph is an increased son, an increased son. And who has been so increased as this one, who after errors and falls has been restored and reinstated through the several steps of the virtues, so as to reach the highest palm? But because he climbed up little by little, he is therefore said to be increased in each one. For he first of all began to be increased through confession in Judah; and again, when he cast off the works of darkness by night, he was increased in Zebulun; and once more he was increased in Issachar, when the reward of his work was augmented. He was increased in Dan, when he preferred right judgement to his own and perverse thoughts. He was increased also in Gad, when, being tempted, he prevailed. He was increased in Asher, when he came to blessedness. Fittingly, then, Joseph is now also called an increased son, he who now obtains the good things of the age to come. And as for his being called an envied son, it means that he is to be imitated by the good, but pursued with envy and slanders by the wicked. Of this good and bad zeal the Apostle also gives indication, when he says of the bad zeal of the Jews: They are zealous for you, not rightly (Gal. 4). And of good zeal he says of himself: For I am zealous for you with the zeal of God (2 Cor. 11). And he is called a younger son; and why should he not be called younger, who has put off the old man with his deeds, who has risen with Christ and walks in newness of life? And he too is to be named a son for the third time: for his first birth was according to the flesh; the second from conversion, or through baptism; the third is that which is itself also called regeneration, which is resurrection from the dead. For it seems to me that this son is now placed among such as the blessed will be. Therefore he is then told by the father: Return to me. For after the resurrection all who have been set over [others] by God return; and there is also the saying of holy Scripture: Praise no one before his death (Ecclus. 11). And therefore it seems to me the more that so great a blessedness belongs only to one who, after death, has already risen from death. And as to what he says, Against whom they took counsel and reviled: not 'they revile' but 'they reviled', when you were tempted while placed in the flesh in this world. And the lords of the bows laid snares (Ps. 10): those, no doubt, who sit in ambush to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart. But their bows were broken with might, with the might of Jacob. He breaks the bows of the enemies who not only admits no arrow of the devil into himself, but also defends others from his darts and wounds. And the sinews of the arms of their hands are loosened by the hand of the mighty one of Jacob: when he who was mighty in Jacob, and helped him in the struggle, who strengthened Israel so that he made him see God with the mind, helped this one too, and blessed [him] with the blessing of heaven from on high, and the blessing of the earth that holds all things (Ps. 141). For he received not only the inheritance of the earth, as one who is meek, but as one poor in spirit he also obtains the kingdom of heaven. And that earth which holds all things is Christ, which the righteous man receives as his inheritance, and says to the Lord: My portion in the land of the living. And what is the reason on account of which he deserved to obtain these things? Because of the blessing, he says, of the breasts and the womb. The blessing of whose womb, or of whose breasts? Perhaps of that womb which Paul indicates, saying: My little children, with whom I am again in labour (Gal. 4). From this it is clear that there is an apostolic womb, which not only gives birth to sons, but, if perhaps they have turned aside from the truth, takes them back again and is in labour with them a second time. From this womb, then, every righteous man is either born, or, if he is already perfect, he himself both bears sons and nonetheless sucks the apostolic breasts, or even offers them to those who suck, of which the Apostle said: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor. 3); and elsewhere, to express the apostolic breasts more pointedly, he adds: But I was among you as if a nurse were cherishing her children (1 Thess. 2). So the perfection of blessing comes to each righteous man because of the apostolic womb and breasts. And because of the blessing, he says, of your father and your mother. The Father of the perfect is Christ, as he himself also said: Little children, yet a little while I am with you (John 13); and the mother is the Church. This blessing prevailed in the blessings of the abiding mountains and the everlasting hills, that is, of those who pursue knowledge and sublime and lofty works. These blessings will be, he says, upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the brothers over whom he was set. Not only, he says, is the head of the righteous man, which is Christ, blessed, but also the crown of those over whom he was set: for those who conduct themselves rightly and order themselves flourishingly benefit the faithful too, as the Apostle said: For in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you (1 Tim. 4).
THE BLESSING OF BENJAMIN

1. Benjamin, a ravening wolf, will eat in the morning, and at evening will divide the food. I should like the advocates of the historical [sense] of this account to tell me what of a ravening wolf Benjamin had in him, or how he divides food in the morning and at evening. But in these matters even the Jews themselves, gross of heart, shrink from the affront of the letter; and some refer what is written to the voracity of the altar, as having been built in Benjamin's portion, because the things offered in the morning are divided by the priests in the evening. Others, with various other, albeit fabulous, accounts, nonetheless admit that through these things the coherence of the letter cannot stand.

2. In the Church, however, among very many this opinion is held, that what is written seems able to be referred to the Apostle Paul. This indeed we neither shrink from nor reject, but we try to do as it is written: A wise man, hearing a word, praises it and will add to it. So we too add these things to what has been rightly said of Paul by those before us, which we do not deny. Benjamin, he says, is interpreted 'son of sorrow'; by the lot of inheritance he received that place in which the earthly Jerusalem, bearing the type and form of that heavenly Jerusalem, is situated. When, therefore, the time comes for the heavenly Jerusalem, and the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, to be made manifest, then this Jerusalem which is now cast off and rejected because of unbelief, with her sons, having suffered for a long time the hunger for the word of God and spiritual thirst, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, according to the Apostle's promise, then all Israel will be saved, which is now signified under the person of Benjamin. So the last son, Benjamin, obtains the last blessing, because he is also the last to be saved. And he is called a ravening wolf: 'wolf' because of his greed, for he comes from great hunger and want of the word of God; 'ravening', because he too seizes the kingdom of God by force. He will eat in the morning: by 'still morning' I think that time is recalled when he received the law; for then a certain illumination of knowledge was first given to the world, from which the day of knowledge should be believed to have taken, as it were, its beginning. So he still eats in the morning the food he had received in the morning; he eats still, and meditates, following the law of righteousness, [though] he has not attained to the law. At evening he divides the food. This evening is that last time in which he is converted, just as for us too this time of our conversion, in which we now are, is called evening. Then, therefore, he divides the food: for then he understands that in the law the letter must be divided from the spirit, and then he recognises that The letter kills, but the spirit gives life. Since, then, now enlightened by the grace of the Lord, he begins in the law to divide and separate spiritual things from bodily ones, he is therefore said to divide the food at evening, which, though meditating on the law all day, he did not do before.

3. The third sense, however, is almost lacking to us in this place, because that man of ours who was created according to God, who first in Reuben, and Simeon and Levi had gone astray through the threefold movements of the soul; who in Judah, having recognised his error, confesses and repents; who in Zebulun puts off the old man with his deeds; who in Issachar also awaits the reward of good works; who in Dan received the grace of judging and separating good from evil, and of discerning thoughts and spirits; who in Gad is also found approved in temptations; who in Asher also divides food for princes, that is, has served a banquet to all those set over wisdom; who in Naphtali has now received the mysteries either of the vine or of the tree; who in Joseph, arriving at the perfect and highest [state], now holds the glory of the age to come and of the resurrection: what further remains in Benjamin, if not that, after he has, like a hungry and ravening wolf, seized the kingdom of heaven, and has fallen upon those things which he had read in the Law and the Prophets and the Gospels, of which he had knowledge here in part (for the Apostle Paul too says that he has it in part), and, placed in the world as in the morning, he ate, since he lived not by bread alone but also by every word of God: he, placed there in the kingdom, now no longer through a glass in a riddle but face to face, looks upon all these things, and divides and discerns [them], and there at last understands which things in the holy Scriptures were written on account of the present state of life; which have signified the glory of the kingdom to come; which were said on account of the inner man, which on account of the outer man; there he will certainly know more fully which things, among these very things on which we now knock step by step, keep faith with history; which contain mysteries alone; and which ought to be expounded according to the ethical and moral interpretation of Scripture. And if we, poor in the grace of knowledge and still placed in the flesh, have been able to explain these things less than worthily, you will grant pardon; for it is your exceeding charity that makes us dare to bring out our very lack of skill in public: and if I did not obey it, I would count it a very great fault in myself.
